key_terms.term: Torsional shear stress in a solid shaft
key_terms.meaning: τ = 16T/(πd³), where T is torque in N·mm and d is shaft diameter in mm

key_terms.term: Bending stress in a solid shaft
key_terms.meaning: σb = 32M/(πd³), where M is the bending moment in N·mm at the section under study
Te = √(M² + T²); the torque that alone causes the same maximum shear stress as M and T acting together
Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]; used in the bending equation to fix shaft diameter by the maximum normal stress theory
σa = F/A from axial force F in N; it is added to or subtracted from σb before Te and Me are computed
τallow = 0.30 Syt or 0.18 Sut, whichever is smaller, for a shaft with a keyway under steady load; Syt and Sut in N/mm²
k = di/do, so τ = 16T/(π do³(1 − k⁴)); a hollow shaft carries more torque per kilogram of steel
The product GJ, with angle of twist θ = Tl/(GJ) in radians; G is shear modulus in N/mm², J polar second moment of area in mm⁴, l length in mm
Resistance to bending deflection y, checked at gear and bearing seats against limits the application allows
Speed at which a rotating shaft resonates laterally; Nc = (30/π)√(g/δ) rpm, with g = 9.81 m/s² and static deflection δ in m
Estimates the first critical speed from assumed deflections: ωn = √(g Σwi yi / Σwi yi²), with weights wi in N and deflections yi in m
1/Nc² = 1/N1² + 1/N2² + …, combining separate critical speeds of each mass; the result is always lower than the lowest single value
A small steel piece seated half in the shaft and half in the hub; it carries torque by shear and crushing, not by friction
The slot cut in the shaft and hub to hold the key; it removes material and adds stress concentration
Integral axial teeth on the shaft matching grooves in the hub; used where the hub must slide along the shaft under load
A rigid coupling: two flanges keyed to the two shafts and bolted together, with no allowance for misalignment
A coupling whose pins carry rubber bushes; the bush deflection absorbs small parallel, angular and axial misalignment
T = μ W rf n, where μ is friction coefficient, W total axial clamping force in N, rf friction radius in mm and n the number of friction faces
Assumes p·r = constant across the friction face, giving rf = (ro + ri)/2; the standard assumption for clutches and brakes after running-in
Rate of heat generated = Tω watts, with T in N·m and ω in rad/s; the drum must radiate and absorb this without overheating

takeaways: A transmission shaft usually carries bending and torsion at the same time, so its diameter is fixed from the equivalent torque or equivalent bending moment, not from either load alone.
The ASME code lowers the allowable shear stress to 0.30 Syt or 0.18 Sut to cover keyway stress concentration and mild shock, so a code-designed shaft is larger than a purely theoretical one.
A hollow shaft with ratio k has (1 − k⁴) less material doing the same work, which is why large marine and turbine shafts are bored out.
Strength alone is not enough: twist, lateral deflection and critical speed must be checked, because a strong shaft can still vibrate or misalign the gears it carries.
Keep the running speed at least about 25 percent away from the first critical speed, and remember Dunkerley's value is always on the safe (low) side.
A key fails in shear along the shaft-hub interface or in crushing on its side face; the shorter of the two lengths decides the key length.
Splines replace the key where torque is large or the hub must move; they spread the load over many teeth and avoid a single deep keyway.
A rigid coupling demands good alignment and is cheap; a flexible coupling costs more but protects bearings from misalignment, thermal growth and shock.
A clutch and a brake are the same friction problem seen twice: one joins two moving parts smoothly, the other turns kinetic energy into heat that must be removed.
In both clutches and brakes, uniform wear theory is the design case and uniform pressure theory is the limiting new-lining case.
bank_note: Long answers here are expected to run a full design calculation — loads, equivalent torque or moment, material and allowable stress, then the diameter or length — and to add the rigidity, critical-speed or heat-dissipation check that the question hints at.

bank.q: Derive the expressions for equivalent torque and equivalent bending moment for a shaft carrying a bending moment M and a torque T simultaneously. State the failure theory behind each.
outline: Draw the stress element: bending stress σb = 32M/(πd³) and torsional shear τ = 16T/(πd³)
Write principal stresses from the two-dimensional state
Apply maximum shear stress theory to get τmax = (16/πd³)√(M² + T²), giving Te
Apply maximum normal stress theory to get σmax = (32/πd³)·½[M + √(M² + T²)], giving Me
Say which theory is conservative and which is used by the ASME code

bank.q: Why must a shaft be checked for rigidity when it is already strong enough? Explain torsional and lateral rigidity and the practical limits placed on each.
outline: Twist θ = Tl/(GJ); too much twist upsets gear mesh and timing
Deflection and slope at gears and bearings: limits chosen by the application, not by strength
Long shafts and shafts of small diameter are the usual offenders
Effect on bearing life, gear contact pattern, vibration and noise
Mention critical speed as the extreme case of a flexible shaft

bank.q: With neat sketches, describe the common types of keys and explain the two ways a key can fail.
outline: Sunk key: square, rectangular, taper and parallel varieties; w and t relations to shaft diameter
Woodruff key: half disc, self-aligning, used on tapered shafts
Kennedy and round keys for light duty
Shear failure: τ = 2T/(d·w·l) over the shaft-hub interface
Crushing failure: σc = 4T/(d·t·l) on the side face
Take the smaller of the two lengths; state the usual proportions of w and t

bank.q: Compare rigid and flexible couplings. Sketch a protected flange coupling and a bushed-pin coupling and say where each is chosen.
outline: Rigid: flange coupling, two flanges keyed and bolted, no misalignment allowed
Design checks: bolt shear, bolt crushing, hub torsion, key, flange bearing
Flexible: bushed-pin, Oldham, universal joint, and their misalignment capabilities
Cost, alignment tolerance, shock absorption, maintenance
Applications: rigid for line shafts on a common bed; flexible for motor to gearbox

bank.q: Explain uniform pressure and uniform wear theories for a friction clutch. Derive the friction radius for each and state which one a designer uses.
outline: Axial force W, inner radius ri, outer radius ro, μ, n friction pairs
Uniform pressure: p constant, T = (2/3)μW n (ro³ − ri³)/(ro² − ri²)
Uniform wear: p·r = C, T = ½ μW n (ro + ri)
Wear theory is the running condition; pressure theory is the new lining
Typical assumption ro/ri about 1.25 to 1.5 and why

bank.q: A solid shaft of 60 mm diameter transmits 25 kW at 400 rpm while carrying a bending moment of 900 N·m at the critical section. Using the ASME code with Syt = 250 N/mm² and Sut = 450 N/mm², find the factor of safety on the maximum shear stress theory.
outline: T = 60×10⁶ P/(2πN) with P in kW, N in rpm, giving T in N·mm
τallow = min(0.30 Syt, 0.18 Sut) = 75 N/mm²
τmax = (16/πd³)√(M² + T²)
Compare induced τmax with τallow, report the factor of safety
Comment that a keyway would require a larger diameter or a reduced allowable stress

bank.q: A solid shaft and a hollow shaft of the same outside diameter must transmit the same torque at the same allowable shear stress. Find the ratio of their weights for di/do = 0.6 and comment on the result.
outline: τ = 16T/(πdo³(1 − k⁴)) for the hollow shaft
Same τ and do means the hollow shaft carries (1 − k⁴) less torque, so for equal torque the hollow shaft needs a larger do
Alternatively, for equal torque the hollow shaft is lighter by the factor (1 − k²)
Numbers for k = 0.6 and a short practical comment on cost of boring

bank.q: A shaft carries a 400 N rotor at mid-span and a 250 N pulley at one-third span. The static deflections at these points are 0.25 mm and 0.10 mm. Estimate the first critical speed by Rayleigh's method and check it by Dunkerley's method.
outline: Rayleigh: ωn = √(g Σwy/Σwy²), convert mm to m
Dunkerley: 1/Nc² = 1/N1² + 1/N2² with each mass taken alone
Show Rayleigh gives a slightly higher value and Dunkerley a lower one
State the design rule: keep the running speed clear of Nc by a safe margin
Mention that gyroscopic and bearing stiffness effects are ignored

bank.q: A 50 mm shaft transmits 40 kW at 500 rpm to a hub through a square key. Taking the allowable shear stress in the key as 40 N/mm² and the crushing stress as 80 N/mm², find the required key length.
outline: T from power and speed, in N·mm
Key proportions w = t = d/4 = 12.5 mm
Shear: l = 2T/(d·w·τ)
Crushing: l = 4T/(d·t·σc)
Take the larger length, add a small margin for the hub length

bank.q: Design a protected flange coupling for a 30 kW, 720 rpm motor shaft of 45 mm diameter: number and size of bolts, flange thickness, hub dimensions and key. State every assumption.
outline: Torque and design torque with a service factor
Bolt circle diameter as about 3d, number of bolts from the standard count
Bolt shear and crushing checks
Hub torsional and crushing check, flange shear check
Key and its length; state the material and allowable stresses used

bank.q: A single plate clutch with both sides effective must transmit 15 kW at 1000 rpm. Coefficient of friction 0.3, maximum pressure 0.1 N/mm², ro/ri = 1.4. Find ri and ro on uniform wear theory and the axial spring force needed.
outline: T from power and speed
Uniform wear: T = μW n (ro + ri)/2 and W = 2πp ri (ro − ri)
Solve the two equations for ri and ro
Check the resulting p on the inner radius
Comment on the effect of n = 2 and on heat generated

bank.q: A shaft that is strong enough on paper keeps cracking at the keyway within weeks of service. Analyse the possible causes and recommend design changes, taking both strength and rigidity into account.
outline: Keyway stress concentration factor and the notch sensitivity of the material
Fatigue: fluctuating torque, S-N curve, endurance limit reduction
Check ASME allowable stress for keyed shafts and the effect of shock factors
Rigidity and critical speed as secondary contributors to vibration
Fixes: larger diameter, end-milled keyway with round ends, splines, fillets, better material

bank.q: A motor drives a gearbox whose shaft centre is 0.3 mm off and 0.2° skewed. Evaluate the choice between a rigid flange coupling and a flexible bushed-pin coupling, including the effect on critical speed and bearing life.
outline: Rigid coupling forces the misalignment into the bearings as a radial load
Flexible coupling absorbs it through bush deflection, with a stated limit
Bearing life falls sharply with added radial load
Misalignment stiffness changes the system natural frequency; check the margin from the running speed
Cost, maintenance, alignment quality at installation as the decision factors

bank.q: Compare the design of a multi-plate clutch and a block brake of similar size. Discuss which assumptions carry over between them and why the brake has an extra thermal check.
outline: Same friction pair analysis: μ, W, rf, n; uniform wear versus uniform pressure
Clutch slips briefly at start; brake may slip for a long descent
Heat generated Tω must be absorbed and radiated; temperature rise and fade
Material choice: clutch lining for wear life, brake lining for hot strength
Failure consequences and factor of safety choices

glossary.def: A rotating machine element of circular cross-section that transmits power and supports pulleys, gears or rotors.
A shaft-like element that supports rotating parts but transmits no torque.
A turning moment in N·mm or N·m, equal to force times the perpendicular distance from the axis.
J = πd⁴/32 for a solid round shaft; it measures resistance to twist, in mm⁴.
The shear stress set up across a shaft section by torque, largest at the outer surface.
The normal stress on a plane where shear stress is zero; found from σb and τ acting together.
A failure criterion saying yield occurs when the largest shear stress reaches the shear yield strength; used to get equivalent torque.
A failure criterion saying failure occurs at the largest principal normal stress; it gives the equivalent bending moment.
Kt = peak stress divided by nominal stress, caused by a notch, hole, shoulder or keyway.
The stress amplitude below which a steel specimen survives indefinitely in reversed fatigue loading.
The bending deflection of a shaft under its own weight and the weight of the parts it carries, used to estimate critical speed.
Large lateral vibration of a rotating shaft when its speed approaches a natural frequency.
The frequency in cycles per second at which a system oscillates freely after a disturbance.
A multiplier applied to the nominal torque to allow for shock and duty of the driven machine.
A removable metal piece that locks a hub to a shaft so they rotate together.
The machined slot in a shaft or hub that receives a key.
One of several integral axial teeth on a shaft that engage matching grooves in a hub.
A device that joins two shaft ends and passes torque from one to the other.
Departure from a common axis of two shafts, either parallel offset, angular or a combination.
A flexible coupling with a cross-shaped spider that allows a large working angle between shafts.
A device that connects or disconnects two rotating parts while running, by friction or by positive engagement.
A device that slows or stops a rotating part by absorbing its kinetic energy as heat.
The single radius at which the total friction force may be assumed to act, giving T = μWrf.
Loss of braking or clutch effectiveness when the lining overheats.
